title: Players Returning from Achilles, ACL and Other Major Injuries
brief: What should we expect from players coming back from Achilles tears, ACL tears and other major injuries: timelines, efficiency loss, minutes limits and skipped back-to-backs? It must say how to price them in our H2H league and why the market is often too scared of them.
summary: Players coming back from Achilles and ACL tears usually return close to their old level, but in the first season back they lose efficiency, play on minutes limits and sit back-to-backs. The draft market fears them more than the risk deserves. In our 9-cat H2H auction, bid on them at a discount, but plan for fewer games and weaker FG% early, and remember that our playoffs (weeks 19 to 21, ending 2027-03-28) come late in the ramp-up.

sections.heading: Timelines: count the months before you bid

paragraphs.text: A full Achilles tear usually takes 9 to 12 months to heal, and closer to 12 is more common. A partial tear takes about 6 months. Before the draft on 2026-10-18, check the date of each player's tear. Count forward to opening week and to our playoff weeks. A player who tore his Achilles less than 9 months before the season should be treated as a likely early IL stash, not a starter.

A full 12 months or more off after an Achilles tear may help a player come back stronger than a 9 to 11 month return. So a slow return is not a red flag on its own. It can be a good sign for the second half of our season and the playoffs.

A normal ACL return takes about 12 months. A player who is more than 12 months past a torn ACL at the start of the season can be treated as fully healthy. If he is under 12 months, expect a managed first stretch. Players who rely on IQ and strength come back from an ACL better than players who rely on speed and explosiveness. The note gives Zach LaVine as an example of the speed type.

sections.heading: What the first season back looks like

paragraphs.text: Expect three things. First, minutes limits. Second, skipped back-to-backs. Third, a drop in efficiency. Injuries have a hidden cost on top of the missed games: during the ramp-up the player is on limited minutes, so all of his counting stats drop at the same time.

Achilles returnees almost never play both games of a back-to-back. Over the last 10 years only Wes Matthews really did it, and he played heavily reduced minutes in the second game. ACL returnees also usually sit back-to-backs early on. Older players returning from major injuries are the most likely to sit them early in the season.

The efficiency loss hits our league in a specific place. Achilles returnees tend to lose efficiency on two-point shots and finishing. FG% is a team ratio, so a high-volume returnee who scores near the rim can pull our FG% down more than a low-volume player would. When you plan a build, do not count on such a player to carry FG% in the first months. Lean on his other categories instead.

The experts disagree on how big the long-term drop is. One view: recent Achilles returnees have mostly come back close to their old level, and the old rule of an automatic 10% career-long drop no longer holds. The other view: players coming back from ACL or Achilles tears almost always lose efficiency in their first season back, especially on two-point shots and finishing. The two views fit together. Expect a weaker first season, mostly in efficiency, but do not mark the player down for the rest of his career.

Achilles returnees carry a risk of compensation injuries elsewhere in the body. Another note says soreness on the other side after major lower-body surgery is common and does not by itself make a player injury-prone. If you own one, do not panic-drop him over one report of soreness on the other side. Use one of our 4 IL slots and wait.

Treat a player with a history of many injuries differently. Some players lose production for a long time even after a minor injury. Those injury-prone players can hurt you long after the injury itself. Give a bigger discount to a returnee who also has a long injury history than to one whose only issue is a single major tear.

Experts differ on how much the schedule matters. One note says returnees may sit back-to-backs, so teams with many back-to-backs hurt them more. Another says back-to-back counts matter mostly for injury-prone players. A third says most back-to-back problems come from in-season injuries that nobody can predict. In practice, check team back-to-back counts only for the major-injury returnees on your list. Do not let the schedule move your price on healthy players.

We set lineups daily, so a skipped game is a lost game unless you fill the slot. If you roster a returnee, keep one bench spot or a waiver pickup ready for his team's back-to-back nights. You have 6 acquisitions per week. Spend some of them on players whose teams play on the nights your returnee rests.

sections.heading: How to price them in our auction

paragraphs.text: Drafters are too scared of players coming back from injuries that cost them last season. You can be more confident than their ADPs suggest. In our auction that means letting others pass on these players, then bidding at the discount the room creates. Do not pay full healthy value either. Take off enough for minutes limits, skipped back-to-backs and weaker FG% early in the season.

Use the timeline to decide how much to pay. A player more than 12 months past an ACL tear can be priced close to his healthy value. An Achilles returnee near the 12-month mark should get a clear discount for the early ramp-up. Still, his value should rise toward weeks 19 to 21, and those are the weeks that decide our title. A player still months from returning on draft day belongs in a cheap end-of-auction bid that you can park on IL.

Favour returnees whose game is built on IQ and strength over those who depend on speed. Among Achilles returnees, prefer players whose value comes from threes, assists, rebounds or free throws over players who rely on finishing at the rim, since finishing is where the efficiency drops.
Older prospects who missed their rookie year to injury get pushed down draft boards. Like other returnees, they can be fair late targets when the room underrates them.

When an older returnee sits back-to-backs early in the season, his backup gets those games. Note the backups behind major-injury returnees. They make good waiver adds for back-to-back nights early in the season, and they can be cheap last-round flyers.

The ramp-up hurts most early in the season, and the restrictions usually ease over time. If a returnee's slow start pushes his owner to sell, try to trade for him before the 2027-03-04 deadline. If you own one who is still restricted near the deadline and you need games in weeks 19 to 21, think about selling him to a manager who values his name.
